summary: Jesus drives the traders out of the temple, calls it a house of prayer made a den of thieves, heals the blind and lame there, and welcomes children’s praise.
key_insight: Matthew notes who came in once the traders were gone: “the blind and the lame came to Him in the temple, and He healed them.” An old saying from David’s day ran, “The blind and the lame shall not come into the house” (2 Samuel 5:8). The Son of David opened the house to them.
story: The next morning Jesus came into Jerusalem and went into the temple. He began to drive out those who bought and sold there. He overturned the tables of the money changers and the seats of those who sold doves, and He would not allow anyone to carry wares through the temple. {Mk}
Then He taught them: “Is it not written, ‘My house shall be called a house of prayer for all nations’? But you have made it a ‘den of thieves.’ ” {Mk}
The blind and the lame came to Him in the temple, and He healed them. Children were crying out in the temple courts, “Hosanna to the Son of David!” {Mt}

When the chief priests and scribes saw the wonderful things He did and heard the children, they were indignant. “Do You hear what these are saying?” they asked. Jesus said to them, “Yes. Have you never read, ‘Out of the mouth of babes and nursing infants You have perfected praise’?” {Mt}

From then on He was teaching daily in the temple. {Lk} The chief priests, the scribes and the leaders of the people looked for a way to destroy Him, for they feared Him, {Mk} but they could do nothing, because all the people were very attentive to hear Him. {Lk} That evening He left the city and went out to Bethany, and He lodged there. {Mt}
differences: Matthew and Luke tell of the clearing right after the entry. Mark says Jesus only looked around the temple that evening and cleared it the next day.
Only Mark says Jesus would not let anyone carry wares through the temple, and only Mark quotes Isaiah in full: “for all nations.”
Only Matthew records the healing of the blind and lame and the children’s “Hosanna to the Son of David!”
Luke tells of the clearing most briefly and adds that Jesus was “teaching daily in the temple” while the people hung on His words.

fit.question: Did Jesus clear the temple on the day He rode into Jerusalem (Matthew, Luke) or the next day (Mark)?

points.label: Mark keeps the clock
points.text: Mark marks each day: Jesus looked around the temple late on the day of the entry and went back to Bethany (11:11); “the next day” He passed the fig tree and cleared the temple (11:12, 15); in the morning they found the tree withered (11:20).

points.label: Matthew and Luke do not say “same day”
points.text: Their “Then” (Matthew 21:12; Luke 19:45) is a simple “and” in Greek, which joins events without timing them. Matthew himself shows a night passed before the fig tree: “Now in the morning, as He returned to the city” (21:18). He and Luke move from the King’s entry to His act in the temple because the one leads to the other.

fit.note: Mark gives the order of days; Matthew and Luke give the order of meaning. Neither claims what the other denies.
fit.short: Mark gives the timing: Jesus looked around on Sunday and cleared the temple Monday. Matthew and Luke join the two scenes without a time note.

scene.label: The court of the nations
scene.text: The market stood in the great outer court, the only part of the temple Gentiles could enter. A stone barrier with warning notices kept them from going farther; two of those inscriptions have been found, threatening death to any foreigner who passed. Jesus quoted Isaiah’s promise that God’s house would be “a house of prayer for all nations” (Isaiah 56:7) in the one court where the nations could pray.

scene.label: Seats of the dove sellers
scene.text: Doves were the offering of the poor, who could not afford a lamb (Leviticus 12:8; compare Luke 2:24). A tradition in the Mishnah tells of a time when a pair of doves in Jerusalem cost so much that a leading rabbi stepped in to bring the price down (Keritot 1:7).

scene.label: A den of thieves
scene.text: Jesus borrowed Jeremiah’s words from his sermon at the temple gate (Jeremiah 7:1–11). People were stealing, lying and worshiping idols, then coming to the temple and feeling safe. A den is where robbers hide after a robbery. Jeremiah warned that God would destroy that temple as He had Shiloh, and He did.

scene.label: No shortcut
scene.text: A later Jewish rule in the Mishnah forbids using the Temple Mount as a shortcut through the city (Berakhot 9:5). Mark says Jesus would not let anyone carry goods through the courts, as though the house of God were a street.

scene.label: “Out of the mouth of babes”
scene.text: Jesus quoted Psalm 8:2. Matthew gives it in the wording of the Greek Old Testament, “perfected praise,” where the Hebrew reads “ordained strength.” Psalm 8 is about praise to God. The leaders wanted Jesus to silence praise of Himself; He answered with a psalm about praise God Himself has prepared.

witnesses.matthew: Moves from the entry straight into the temple and adds what happened once the traders were gone: the blind and lame healed and children shouting “Hosanna to the Son of David!” The King of David’s line acts as Lord of the house.
witnesses.mark: Gives the clearest timetable and frames the scene with the fig tree. He alone records that Jesus stopped people carrying goods through the courts and quotes Isaiah’s full line, “a house of prayer for all nations.”
witnesses.luke: Tells of the clearing in two verses and turns at once to Jesus teaching daily in the temple. Luke’s Gospel begins and ends in the temple (1:9; 24:53), and here the cleared temple becomes Jesus’ classroom.
witnesses.john: Does not record this event. He tells of a clearing of the temple at the first Passover of Jesus’ ministry (John 2:13–22). Many hold that Jesus cleared the temple twice; others think John placed the one cleansing for its meaning. Views differ (see event 24).

seeing.reveals: Jesus acts as Lord of the temple. He clears out the trade, opens the house to the blind and the lame, and accepts the children’s praise with a psalm about praise to God.
seeing.living: Jesus cared about who could get in. The market filled the one court where the nations could pray, and the blind and the lame came in once He had cleared it. Ask what in your worship, or your church’s habits, makes it hard for outsiders and broken people to come near God, and let Him clear it away.
seeing.ponder: Who is still kept at the edge of the place where you worship, and would Jesus’ house have room for them?

preaching.big_idea: Jesus clears His Father’s house to make room for those who were kept out.
outline: A house opened to the broken (14)
preaching.watch_for: Matthew sets two Scripture quotations side by side (vv. 13, 16): Isaiah and Jeremiah on what the temple had become, and Psalm 8 on the praise God prepares. The leaders are indignant at the healings and the praise alike (v. 15).
